title: When to see a fertility doctor
tagline: How long to try first, and when not to wait

sources.label: ASRM — Fertility Evaluation of Infertile Women, Committee Opinion (2026)

sections.heading: The usual timeline
sections.body: If you have regular unprotected sex with a male partner and no known fertility problem, the recommendation is to get evaluated after 12 months of trying if you are under 35, and after 6 months if you are 35 or older. Over 40, it often makes sense to start sooner.

sections.heading: Reasons not to wait
sections.body: Start right away if your cycles are shorter than 25 or longer than 35 days, you bleed between periods or don't have periods, you've had repeated pregnancy losses, you have known or suspected endometriosis or problems with your uterus or tubes, your partner may have sperm problems, or you've had chemotherapy or radiation.

sections.heading: Planning ahead
sections.body: You can also be seen right away if you're planning egg freezing, using donor eggs or sperm, or planning genetic testing of embryos.

sections.heading: Age matters most
sections.body: Age is the single strongest predictor of fertility, which is why the waiting time is shorter after 35.

ask: I'm 36 and we've been trying for 7 months. Should I see someone?

title: Your first evaluation, test by test

sources.label: ASRM — Fertility Evaluation of Infertile Women, Committee Opinion (2026)

sections.heading: The four core questions
sections.body: A fertility evaluation looks at whether you ovulate, the shape of your uterus, whether your fallopian tubes are open, and, with a male partner, a semen analysis. Both partners are evaluated at the same time, since sperm-related factors play a part in up to 40% of cases.

sections.heading: Your history
sections.body: Your doctor will ask about your cycles, past pregnancies, health, medicines, family history and lifestyle. A routine pelvic exam is usually not needed if you have a pelvic ultrasound.

sections.heading: Checking the uterus
sections.body: A transvaginal ultrasound is the best first test. A saline ultrasound (sonohysterography) is very accurate for finding polyps or fibroids inside the uterus, and hysteroscopy (a small camera) can both find and treat them.

sections.heading: Checking the tubes
sections.body: Most people have an HSG (an X-ray with dye) or a HyCoSy (an ultrasound with contrast); both are similarly accurate. If one tube looks blocked near the uterus, there's more than a 40% chance it's actually open on later testing, so a second test is sometimes needed.

sections.heading: Tests you usually don't need
sections.body: Postcoital tests, endometrial biopsy, temperature charting, and routine thyroid, prolactin, clotting, immune or chromosome tests are not routinely recommended unless there's a specific reason. Your doctor orders a test when it would change your care.

title: AMH and ovarian reserve
tagline: What your egg count tests can and can't tell you

sources.label: ASRM — Fertility Evaluation of Infertile Women, Committee Opinion (2026)

sections.heading: What the tests are
sections.body: Ovarian reserve tests estimate how many eggs you have. They include AMH (a blood test you can take on any day of your cycle), FSH and estradiol on cycle days 2 to 4, and an ultrasound count of small follicles called the antral follicle count.

sections.heading: What they're used for
sections.body: Their main job is to predict how your ovaries will respond to fertility medicines, so your doctor can plan treatment and set expectations.

sections.heading: What AMH doesn't tell you
sections.body: AMH reflects how many eggs you have, not their quality. On its own it is poor at predicting whether you can get pregnant naturally, and a low AMH should never be used to exclude you from treatment.

sections.heading: One test is enough
sections.body: AMH varies a little within a cycle, so repeat testing isn't recommended. One result, read together with your age and history, is the standard. Age is still the strongest predictor of fertility.

title: LGBTQ+, single parents and donor sperm
tagline: Your path doesn't start with a year of trying

sources.label: ASRM — Fertility Evaluation of Infertile Women, Committee Opinion (2026)

sections.heading: No waiting period
sections.body: Single women, same-sex female couples and others using donor sperm get a targeted evaluation instead of having to 'try' first. Transgender and nonbinary patients get an evaluation tailored to them.

sections.heading: Fair access
sections.body: Guidance from the American Society for Reproductive Medicine is clear that relationship status or sexual orientation should never be used to deny or delay fertility care.

sections.heading: Reciprocal IVF
sections.body: Same-sex couples can choose reciprocal IVF, where one partner's eggs are used and the other partner carries the pregnancy.

sections.heading: Donor sperm in IVF
sections.body: In IVF, donor sperm is thawed on the day of egg retrieval. It is rare for sperm not to survive thawing.

title: IVF step by step

sections.heading: 1. Stimulation
sections.body: Injectable medicines help several follicles (the fluid sacs that hold eggs) grow at once.

sections.heading: 2. Monitoring
sections.body: Blood tests and ultrasounds, sometimes daily, track how you're responding.

sections.heading: 3. Trigger shot
sections.body: When the follicles are ready, you give yourself an injection that matures the eggs.

sections.heading: 4. Egg retrieval
sections.body: 34 to 36 hours later, the eggs are collected under sedation. You go home the same day.

sections.heading: 5. Fertilization
sections.body: In the lab, eggs are fertilized with standard insemination or ICSI (one sperm injected into each egg).

sections.heading: 6. Embryo transfer
sections.body: 3 or 5 days after retrieval, one or more embryos are placed in the uterus through a thin catheter.

sections.heading: 7. After transfer
sections.body: Progesterone supports implantation, usually until about week 8 of pregnancy after a fresh transfer. Good-quality extra embryos can be frozen.

title: Stimulation, injections and monitoring

sections.heading: Why injections
sections.body: Fertility medicines help several follicles grow and mature at the same time, instead of the usual one. They're given either under the skin (subcutaneous) or into a muscle (intramuscular). Your doctor will go through your exact medicines and how to give them.

sections.heading: Monitoring visits
sections.body: You may come in as often as every day. Each visit usually means a blood draw for hormone levels and a transvaginal ultrasound to measure the follicles.

sections.heading: Common side effects
sections.body: Mild bruising or soreness where you inject, temporary redness or itching, nausea and sometimes vomiting, breast tenderness, more vaginal discharge, mood swings and tiredness are all common.

sections.heading: When a cycle is stopped
sections.body: If your ovaries respond too little, the team will talk with you about other options. If they respond too strongly, there's a risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), and the cycle is cancelled to keep you safe.

call_if: Severe belly pain, trouble breathing or signs of dehydration during or after stimulation (possible severe OHSS).

title: Trigger shot and egg retrieval day

sections.heading: The trigger shot
sections.body: When your doctor says the follicles are ready, you give yourself the trigger injection. Retrieval is scheduled 34 to 36 hours later, so take it at the exact time your clinic gives you.

sections.heading: On the day
sections.body: Retrieval is an outpatient procedure. You receive deep sedation through an IV. Guided by ultrasound, the doctor passes a thin needle through the vaginal wall into each ovary and draws fluid from the follicles. An embryologist then finds the eggs in that fluid.

sections.heading: Safety under sedation
sections.body: Problems from sedation are rare. To lower the rare risk of nerve injury from positioning, your legs are placed in position while you're still awake, and the anesthesia team watches you the whole time.

sections.heading: Recovery
sections.body: Mild to moderate pelvic or belly pain is common and usually settles in 1 to 2 days. Over-the-counter pain relievers usually help.

sections.heading: Rare cancellations
sections.body: Very occasionally retrieval is cancelled shortly before, for example if ovulation happens too early or hormone levels drop.

call_if: Pain that is severe or getting worse instead of better after 1 to 2 days.
Fever or signs of infection after retrieval.

title: Fertilization, embryos and transfer
tagline: What happens in the lab and after

sections.heading: Two ways to fertilize
sections.body: With standard insemination, sperm are placed with the eggs and enter them on their own. With ICSI, an embryologist injects one sperm into each egg. ICSI costs more and is used when standard insemination looks less likely to work.

sections.heading: Genetic testing
sections.body: If embryos are tested (preimplantation genetic testing), a laser makes a small opening in the embryo's shell first. This is called assisted hatching.

sections.heading: The transfer
sections.body: 3 or 5 days after retrieval, embryos are placed in the uterus with a thin catheter through the cervix. You may feel mild cramping or have slight spotting. Your team may suggest a practice (mock) transfer beforehand.

sections.heading: How many embryos
sections.body: The number depends on your age, embryo quality and other factors. The goal is the best chance of pregnancy with the lowest chance of twins or triplets.

sections.heading: After the transfer
sections.body: Progesterone, by injection or vaginally, helps the embryo implant and usually continues until about week 8 of pregnancy after a fresh transfer. Good-quality extra embryos, at 5 to 7 days old, can be frozen. Never stop or change progesterone without asking your care team.

title: Egg freezing

sources.label: ASRM — Fertility Evaluation of Infertile Women, Committee Opinion (2026)

sections.heading: Who freezes eggs
sections.body: People freeze eggs before cancer treatment, because of a chronic illness, or to delay having children. If you're planning egg freezing, you can be evaluated right away.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Egg freezing follows the first half of IVF: stimulation, monitoring, the trigger shot and egg retrieval. The eggs are then frozen instead of being fertilized.

sections.heading: What tests help plan it
sections.body: Ovarian reserve tests such as AMH and an antral follicle count help predict how many eggs stimulation is likely to produce.

sections.heading: No guarantees
sections.body: Not every frozen egg survives thawing, and some thawed eggs don't fertilize, so egg freezing improves your options but can't guarantee a future pregnancy.

title: Risks and when to call
tagline: Warning signs to know before you start

sections.heading: OHSS
sections.body: Mild ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome causes nausea, bloating and pelvic discomfort and usually improves within a few days of egg collection. Severe OHSS can cause fluid in the belly and sometimes the lungs. Very rarely it leads to blood clots or kidney failure.

sections.heading: Ectopic pregnancy
sections.body: With IVF, about 1% of pregnancies grow outside the uterus. Treatment is medicine or surgery.

sections.heading: Infection
sections.body: Pelvic infection after retrieval or transfer is uncommon. It's more likely if you've had a pelvic infection before or have endometriosis on an ovary.

sections.heading: Retrieval injuries
sections.body: Rarely, the needle can injure the bladder, bowel or a blood vessel, which may need emergency surgery.

call_if: Trouble breathing, severe belly pain or signs of dehydration.
Sharp or stabbing pain, vaginal bleeding, dizziness, fainting or lower back pain in early pregnancy.
Fever or signs of infection after a procedure.
If it feels like an emergency, call 911.

title: Results, setbacks and next steps
tagline: Honest numbers and what comes next

sections.heading: No guarantees
sections.body: IVF can lead to a pregnancy and leave you with frozen embryos for later, but no step is guaranteed. You decide with your doctor whether the benefits are worth the risks for you.

sections.heading: Miscarriage
sections.body: The chance of miscarriage after IVF is similar to a natural pregnancy and rises with age: about 15% in your 20s and more than 50% in your 40s.

sections.heading: Twins and multiples
sections.body: IVF makes twins or triplets more likely, especially when more embryos are transferred. Multiples carry more risk of premature birth, high blood pressure, gestational diabetes and cesarean delivery.

sections.heading: Birth defects
sections.body: Birth defects affect 2% to 3% of all babies. The rate is slightly higher with fertility problems, mostly because of age and the cause of infertility; it's not clear IVF itself raises it. Newer, high-quality studies show no clear link between fertility medicines and ovarian cancer.

sections.heading: If a cycle doesn't work
sections.body: A cancelled cycle or a negative result is not the end of the road. Your doctor will review what happened and talk through other options with you.

title: You don't have to do this alone

sources.label: RESOLVE: The National Infertility Association — support groups

sections.heading: It's normal to struggle
sections.body: Fertility treatment is physically and emotionally demanding, for you and for anyone going through it with you. Feeling anxious, sad or overwhelmed doesn't mean you're doing it wrong.

sections.heading: Talk to your care team
sections.body: Ask your clinic about counseling. Dr Tessa's team can also book a real consultation if you'd like to talk things through.

sections.heading: Support groups
sections.body: RESOLVE: The National Infertility Association runs free peer-led and professionally led support groups, in person and online.

sections.heading: HelpLine
sections.body: RESOLVE's HelpLine is 866-NOT-ALONE (866-668-2566). It's a voicemail line: leave a message on any infertility topic and a trained volunteer calls you back, usually within 1 to 3 days.

call_if: If you're thinking about harming yourself, call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) right away.
